newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-SESTRIERE STEPS INTO THE SPOTLIGHT.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-SESTRIERE STEPS INTO THE SPOTLIGHT.

text.p: Everybody interested in Alpine skiing knows that the world championships begin in Sestriere on Sunday and continue for two weeks.
But they may be puzzled as to why the Italian resort has chosen a white elephant on skis as its mascot.
Alberto Tomba has been a regular here for more than a decade but even the Italian superstar may not know the connection between Sestriere and "War and Peace".
And why do all the posters in shop windows and banners fluttering in the streets proclaim the "Sestrieres" championships when nobody in Italy spells it that way?
First the elephant, or "Annifant".
A bemedalled but otherwise strangely legless creation on golden skis, Annifant recalls ancient history.
Local legend has it that the Carthaginian general Hannibal crossed the Alps near Sestriere in the third century BC with his army and elephants in a failed bid to conquer Rome.
Organisers say his whiteness is all to do with snow and symbolism, making Annifant "happy and cheerful."
Roman armies also camped around the site of the modern resort on their way towards ancient Gaul.
The name itself comes from the Latin "Petra Sistraria", or sixth stone, because in Roman days the isolated plain was the site of the sixth milestone from the nearest settlement.
The area was in subsequent centuries ruled by Saracens, French, Austrians and the royal house of Savoy.
The French, with downhill World Cup champion Luc Alphand living just over the border, and the dominant Austrians will be trying to lay down the law again in the coming 14 days.

The history lesson pretty much ends there for a purpose-built resort whose existence really dates from the 1930s when the Agnelli family, of Fiat car giant fame, decided to develop the plateau for mass recreational skiing.
It was the first resort of its kind in the world.
Giovanni Agnelli senior knew the area well because he had been there from nearby Turin for engine tests.
The main square is "Piazza Agnelli".
Originally called Sestrieres, deriving from local patois rather than French, it became Sestriere in 1935 when the Fascist government of Benito Mussolini Italianised names.
The dual-identity has remained ever since, with locals and outsiders using both spellings in equal measure.
"Be it Sestrieres or Sestriere, it should not be forgotten that the correct pronunciation requires the name to be stressed on the penultimate E," a guidebook explains.
"Unless you want to sound totally unfashionable."

The resort may not be the most trendy in Italy -- Cortina d'Ampezzo has more of a reputation for wealth and glamour nowadays -- but filmstars and sports celebrities were once regular visitors and are sure to be again this month.
"Saint Moritz, Cortina, Davos, Garmisch, St Anton, Zermatt, Chamonix are adaptations. Sestriere is an invention," a history of the resort's first 50 years declares proudly.
In the 1960s, Russian film director Sergei Bondarchuk shot Tolstoy's "War and Peace" on location here.
In the summer months, the Tour de France and Giro d'Italia cycle races have passed through Sestriere while the resort also boasts Europe's highest 18-hole golf course.
The 2,050 metre high station also hosts every year an athletics Grand Prix event at which the prize on offer for a world record is a bright red Ferrari sportscar.
There are no cash prizes for world championship winners. Just a gold medal and a place in history.
